title: Psychology · Episode 2
chapters: Willpower: what the marshmallow test really tells us
Cognitive biases: the shortcuts that fool you

units.t: Psychology. Episode two.
In this episode: How habits really work, Willpower: what the marshmallow test really tells us and Cognitive biases: the shortcuts that fool you.
Part one. How habits really work.
Around 40% of what you do each day happens on autopilot.
Here's how to take control of the autopilot.
Autopilot and the loop.
Studies that asked people to log their day found roughly 40% of actions were repeated almost daily, in the same place, often while thinking about something else.
Habits free your conscious mind, but bad habits run on the same autopilot, which is why willpower alone so often fails.
Researchers describe a habit as a loop.
A cue triggers it: a time, place, feeling, person or preceding action.
The routine is the behaviour itself.
The reward makes the brain want to repeat the loop.
Finishing a coffee, cue, leads to checking your phone, routine, which delivers a hit of novelty, reward.
Charles Duhigg popularised this model in The Power of Habit, and James Clear expanded it in Atomic Habits.
Not 21 days.
You may have heard that habits take 21 days.
That figure doesn't come from habit research.
In a 2009 study at University College London, volunteers chose a new daily behaviour, like drinking water with lunch or doing sit-ups before dinner.
On average it took 66 days for the behaviour to feel automatic, but the range was huge, from 18 to 254 days depending on the person and the habit.
Encouragingly, missing a single day didn't derail progress.
Consistency matters more than perfection.
Obvious and easy.
Vague intentions like 'I'll exercise more' rarely stick.
Specific plans work better: 'I will do X at time Y in place Z.'
Habit stacking attaches a new habit to an existing cue: 'After I pour my morning coffee, I'll write down three priorities.'
Design your surroundings too: the book on your pillow, the running shoes by the door.
Then cut friction, the biggest enemy of a new habit.
Start ridiculously small: one push-up, one page, two minutes of tidying.
The point isn't the push-up; it's becoming someone who shows up every day.
For bad habits, add friction instead: log out of social media, keep snacks in a high cupboard, leave your credit card out of shopping accounts.
Habits follow the path of least resistance.
Rewards and replacing.
The benefits of fitness or savings arrive months or years later, and our brains value distant rewards little.
So add an immediate one: tick a calendar box and watch the chain grow, pair the habit with something you enjoy, or transfer $5 to a 'treat' account each time you skip takeaway.
Streaks work for this reason, which is why this app has one.
To break a bad habit, replace it.
Work out what reward it gives you.
Is afternoon snacking about hunger, boredom or a break from work?
Keep the cue and reward but change the routine, such as a five-minute walk and chat at the 3 pm slump.
Or remove the cue: people who quit smoking often change routines linked to cigarettes, like the morning coffee spot.
Identity beats goals.
Goals are useful for direction, but they end: you run the marathon, then stop running.
Habits that last are often tied to identity.
'I'm trying to quit smoking' is weaker than 'I'm not a smoker.'
'I want to read more' is weaker than 'I'm a reader.'
Every time you do the behaviour, you cast a small vote for that identity.
Start with who you want to become, then choose the tiny daily actions that person would take, and let the results follow.
The key idea: Habits run on a loop of cue, routine and reward, and about 40% of daily actions are habitual.
Part two. Willpower: what the marshmallow test really tells us.
A child, a marshmallow and a promise of two if they can wait.
It became psychology's most famous test of self control, and the real story is more interesting than the legend.
One treat now, or two.
In the late 1960s and early 1970s, psychologist Walter Mischel and colleagues ran experiments at a Stanford University nursery school.
A child sat at a table with a treat such as a marshmallow, pretzel or biscuit.
If they waited until the researcher returned, they got two treats.
If not, they could ring a bell and eat the single treat straight away.
Some children gobbled it immediately; others squirmed, sang or covered their eyes.
Mischel's original aim was to learn which strategies helped children delay.
A 1990 follow-up of teenagers found longer waiters scored higher on the SAT.
The legend grew, though the samples were small and drawn from a privileged university community.
The 2018 replication.
In 2018, Tyler Watts, Greg Duncan and Haonan Quan revisited the idea with a much larger, more diverse sample of several hundred children.
Waiting longer at age four was linked with better academic achievement at fifteen, but only about half as strongly as in the original.
More importantly, once they accounted for family background, home environment and early cognitive skills, the link shrank substantially and much of it disappeared.
A lot of what the test seemed to measure might reflect a child's circumstances rather than a stable inner trait of willpower.
The test still tells us something, but far less than the legend implied.
Is waiting always smart.
A 2013 study by Celeste Kidd and colleagues at the University of Rochester added a twist.
Before the marshmallow test, children were promised better art supplies.
For one group, the researcher returned with them.
For the other, the researcher came back empty-handed with an apology.
Children who had met a reliable adult waited, on average, around four times longer.
If you grow up where promises are often broken and resources can disappear, grabbing what you can now may be a sensible strategy, not a lack of self-control.
Decisions about waiting depend on trust and circumstance, not only on character.
The willpower battery.
Ego depletion was another hugely influential idea.
In a 1998 study, Roy Baumeister and colleagues asked hungry participants to resist freshly baked cookies and eat radishes instead.
The radish eaters then gave up sooner on an unsolvable puzzle than the cookie eaters.
The conclusion was that willpower is a limited resource, like a muscle that tires.
Hundreds of studies followed.
Then in 2016, a coordinated replication across more than twenty labs and over two thousand participants found an effect close to zero.
A later large project led by Kathleen Vohs, one of the original proponents, also found at most a very small effect.
The strong willpower-battery version is now widely doubted.
Strategies, not strength.
Mischel's original research was about strategies.
Children who distracted themselves, looked away or imagined the marshmallow as a fluffy cloud waited longer than those who stared at it.
A 2012 study by Wilhelm Hofmann and colleagues found people with high self-control reported fewer temptations overall.
They arranged their lives so they rarely had to resist.
Angela Duckworth stresses situational strategies: remove temptations and make good choices easier.
Peter Gollwitzer's if-then plans help too: 'If I want a snack after dinner, I will have fruit.'
So do habits and kindness after lapses, since harsh self-criticism can make people quit.
Self-control depends on strategies, environments and trust, all of which can change.
The key idea: The marshmallow test began as a study of strategies for delaying gratification, and was later spun into a story about predicting success.
Part three. Cognitive biases: the shortcuts that fool you.
Your brain makes the same mistakes again and again, in ways psychologists can predict.
Once you know them, you'll spot them everywhere.
Brain shortcuts.
Your brain handles far more information than it can weigh carefully, so it uses mental shortcuts called heuristics.
Usually they work well: you don't calculate the odds before crossing a quiet street.
But in some situations the same shortcuts cause the same mistakes, again and again.
Psychologists call these systematic errors cognitive biases.
Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman popularised the idea in the 1970s, and Kahneman later won a Nobel Prize in economics.
In his 2011 book Thinking, Fast and Slow, he described System 1, which is fast, automatic and gives you a gut feeling, and System 2, which is slow and tiring, like multiplying 17 by 24.
Most biases are System 1 jumping to conclusions that lazy System 2 never checks.
What we believe.
We notice, search for and remember information that supports what we already believe.
Type 'is coffee bad for you' and you'll find reasons to worry; type 'benefits of coffee' and you'll feel reassured.
Social media amplifies this by showing more of what we already engage with.
That's confirmation bias, and it's why facts alone rarely change minds.
Overconfidence is its partner.
In a classic 1981 study of US and Swedish drivers, most rated themselves safer than the median driver, which can't be true for everyone.

In 1999, David Dunning and Justin Kruger found that the lowest scorers on logic and grammar tests overestimated themselves most, though researchers still debate how much of that is a statistical quirk.
We also underestimate how long projects take, even when we've been late before.
Numbers and odds.
The first number you hear pulls later judgements towards it, even when it's irrelevant.
That's anchoring.
In a famous experiment, people spun a rigged wheel that landed on 10 or 65, then estimated the percentage of African countries in the United Nations.
Those who saw 65 guessed much higher.
A 'was $199' tag makes $129 feel like a deal, a $90 bottle makes the $45 wine seem reasonable, and the first salary mentioned often sets the range.
The availability heuristic works differently: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind.
Plane crashes are vivid, so many people fear flying more than driving, though driving is far more dangerous per kilometre.
Shark attacks make headlines; drownings rarely do.
Losses and sunk costs.
Losing feels worse than gaining the same amount feels good.
Research suggests losses weigh roughly twice as heavily, so most people refuse a coin flip that wins $100 or loses $100.
It explains why people hold falling investments hoping to 'get back to even', why free trials work, and why 'Last chance' sells.
A sunk cost is money, time or effort already spent and gone.

The sunk cost fallacy lets it drive your next decision: sitting through a terrible movie because you paid, a company funding a failing project after spending millions, or staying in a hated job because of the years invested.
Only the future matters.
Ask: 'If I were starting fresh today, would I choose this?'
Fighting back.
You can't switch biases off, and knowing about them doesn't make you immune.
But you can build habits that catch them.
Before a big decision, look for evidence against your view and ask: what would convince me I'm wrong?
Write down your own estimate before hearing anyone else's number.
Ask how you'd feel if the choice were framed as a gain instead of a loss.
Check base rates, meaning how often something actually happens out of how many, rather than trusting vivid stories.
For plans, look at how long similar projects really took.
Small speed bumps like these give your slow, careful System 2 a chance to step in.
The key idea: Cognitive biases are predictable errors caused by fast, automatic mental shortcuts.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. In the habit loop, what is the cue?
Answer. The trigger that starts the loop.
Question two. What was the original aim of Mischel's marshmallow experiments?
Answer. To find which strategies help children delay.
Question three. Why do cognitive biases occur?
Answer. Fast mental shortcuts that mislead everyone the same way.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
